articles.title: When should we listen for alien signals? Scientists turn to game theory
articles.dek: Finding a signal from an extraterrestrial civilization takes more than just pointing a telescope in the right direction. We may also need to listen at exactly the right time.
paragraphs: Finding a signal from an extraterrestrial civilization takes more than just pointing a telescope in the right direction. We may also need to listen at exactly the right time.

Scientists at the SETI Institute are trying a new approach to this challenge. They are combining astronomy and game theory to predict when another civilization might decide to send a message to Earth.

Using the SETI Institute's Allen Telescope Array (ATA) at the Hat Creek Radio Observatory in Northern California, researchers have launched a multiyear search focused on a particular location in the sky known as the anti-solar point. Their approach is based on the idea that two civilizations, even without communicating beforehand, might independently identify the same time and place to establish contact.

A new paper, published in The Astronomical Journal and titled "A Large-Scale Technosignature Survey of the Anti-Solar Point with the Allen Telescope Array: Survey Design and Pilot Results," describes the campaign's strategy and presents findings from its first observations.

The pilot study did not find evidence of extraterrestrial technology, but it marked an important milestone: the first observational search of the anti-solar point, putting a decades-old scientific proposal to the test for the first time and establishing a foundation for a much larger survey.
In game theory, a Schelling point is a choice that two parties might independently make when they need to coordinate without communicating.

Imagine you agree to meet someone in New York City but don't set a time or place. Both of you might choose to meet at noon at Grand Central Terminal, since it's a well-known spot and a common meeting place.
The same principle could apply to communication across interstellar distances.

An extraterrestrial civilization that wants to contact Earth might save energy by sending a focused radio signal at a specific time instead of broadcasting all the time in every direction. But how would it pick a time when someone on Earth might be listening?
The research team suggests that the layout of the solar system could give both sides a common reference point.

From certain locations in the galaxy, an observer could detect Earth passing in front of the sun, an event astronomers call a transit. This would reveal not only Earth's existence but also information about its orbit and its position in the sun's habitable zone.

At the midpoint of that transit, Earth would lie directly between the distant observer and the sun. From Earth's perspective, the transmitter would appear in the direction opposite the sun: the anti-solar point.
Because both civilizations could independently recognize this alignment, it offers a possible way to coordinate communication without having exchanged a message.
This idea does not assume that extraterrestrial civilizations exist or that they would use this strategy. Instead, it gives scientists a clear and testable idea about where and when to search.

articles.title: Stone Age hunters in northern Europe may have used poison arrows to hunt big prey
articles.dek: Autumn walks in Britain are glorious, as the foliage changes color and cool, crisp air begins to bite. However, some of these European trees hide a much darker secret.
paragraphs: Autumn walks in Britain are glorious, as the foliage changes color and cool, crisp air begins to bite. However, some of these European trees hide a much darker secret. For example, the yew tree's lovely red arils—the cup-shaped coverings around the seeds—carry toxins that may have been used to poison arrow tips in the past.

A new Danish study in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports has shown that the "smoking gun" is not the poison itself, but the size of the small arrowheads used to deliver the toxin into the hunted animal.
The authors of the latest research examined Danish stone tool technology from the period immediately preceding the arrival of farming in Europe— the Mesolithic .

They argue that the distinctive small size of stone arrow tips from the early Mesolithic period (about 9,000–3,950 B. C. ) suggests they were used to hunt large prey with the help of poisons. The poison has long since vanished, leaving only the stone tip.

Arrows that do not use poison are typically larger, since they need to damage the animal's flesh. But poisoned arrows need only wound a prey animal enough to allow the poison to enter the bloodstream.

There were several poisonous plants available to hunter-gatherers in early Mesolithic Denmark. These include northern water hemlock, European bird cherry, buttercup and bittersweet nightshade, which have been proposed as possible toxins on arrow points.

In contrast, the authors report that stone arrowheads from the middle and later Mesolithic (about 6,400–3,950 B. C. ) are larger and were used to hunt smaller prey. According to the researchers, the sizes of arrowheads used during this period do not indicate poison use.

Surprisingly, poison-assisted hunting is widely known from a variety of archaeological and ethnographic contexts. For example, ricin—which is made from the castor bean plant—has been linked to a 24,000-year-old poison applicator at Border Cave, KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa.

The San and Ju|'hoan people of Namibia use beetle larvae , as well as sap from a succulent plant called the Bushman poison (Adenium boehmianum). Many other toxins remain unidentified, despite their use as a hunting aid being well established.

The oldest direct evidence of the use of poisoned microlithic (small) tools is from a site in Umhlatuzana Rock Shelter in KwaZulu-Natal. The poison is likely to have derived from a bulbous plant native to Africa called Boophone disticha.
The archaeological levels in which these poisoned arrows were recovered have been dated to 60,000 years old , suggesting that this technology has deep roots.

For poison to be effective, a certain set of skills and precautions are vital. Hunters require detailed knowledge of the plant or animal from which the poison can be gathered, the exact way to prepare it, how to concentrate and mix the poison and the best way to employ the toxin without contaminating the meat of your kill.

articles.title: How humans influence fish behavior and why this is important for species conservation
articles.dek: Two recent review articles in the journals Trends in Ecology & Evolution and Fish and Fisheries , to which researchers from the Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and…
paragraphs: Two recent review articles in the journals Trends in Ecology & Evolution and Fish and Fisheries , to which researchers from the Leibniz Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries (IGB) contributed, focus on the influence of humans on the diversity of fish behavior and on how management can help preserve this diversity.

Who would have thought? Although Amazon mollies are genetically identical as clones of their mothers, individual fish systematically differ from one another in their behavior—even when raised under identical conditions. This is true even for juvenile fish. In fact, among all fish species studied to date, there is immense variation among individuals, including shy and bold or social and less social individuals. Researchers refer to these as behavioral types.

Fish account for about half of all vertebrate species and exhibit an impressive diversity of behaviors within populations, between populations of the same species and between populations living in different ecosystems. As with all vertebrates, behavioral diversity in fish arises from the interplay of various factors. These include an animal's internal state (e. g. , hunger level), its genetic makeup, its ability to flexibly adapt its behavior and the external conditions to which it is exposed. And this diversity can be systematically altered by humans.

Robert Arlinghaus, professor of integrative fisheries management at IGB and Humboldt Universität zu Berlin, has been studying the behavior of freshwater fishes for many years. He contributed to the two articles, which provide an overview of how human activities influence fish behavior and how humans exert a selective pressure that differs from natural factors.

Arlinghaus explained, "Human influences on fish behavior include, for example, habitat alteration and disturbance, migration barriers, pollution, the spread of invasive species, intensive and trait-selective fishing, animals escaped from aquaculture and climate-driven shifts in ecological processes. These so-called anthropogenic factors can directly or indirectly influence activity and movement, reproductive behavior, reactions to predators, aggression, social behavior, cognition and learning."

One example of this is the selection of certain behavioral traits caused by fishing. Previous studies by the IGB have shown that, in recreational fishing, it is primarily the bold and active carp and pike that are removed from the populations. In heavily fished aquatic ecosystems, shyness can therefore be an evolutionary advantage and become established over generations. "However, this also means that fish in heavily fished areas no longer swim around as actively. This can alter the distribution of fish, the relationships between predators and prey, and competitive dynamics," said Arlinghaus.
Fish ladders at hydroelectric power plants can also select for certain behaviors, such as the ability to sprint, and thus lead to behavioral differences among subpopulations below and above dams.

Studies by Swedish researchers involving various fish species have demonstrated that environmental pollution influences fish behavior. For instance, guppies exposed to a realistic environmental concentration of a pharmaceutical contaminant known to reduce human anxiety exhibited a uniform level of activity. Variations in activity levels among individuals dropped to less than half of those observed in unexposed fish. Perch and salmon exposed to pharmaceutical residues as well as cocaine swam more actively in lakes, making them more likely to be eaten.

Artificial light at night is an example of nonmaterial pollution of water bodies. It can also rearrange the interactions between species. For example, small invertebrates gather in illuminated areas of aquatic ecosystems, which in turn alters the feeding behavior and habitat selection of fish.

Another example is the genetic impact of escaped farmed salmon in Norwegian fjords. Salmon return to their native rivers to spawn. This locally adapted behavior can be lost through interbreeding with domesticated farmed salmon that escaped from net cages used for aquaculture.

Whether behavioral diversity is maintained also depends on the state of the ecosystem in question. "In diverse and ecologically challenging habitats, behavioral diversity is often particularly high, as individuals specialize in different resources or strategies," said Arlinghaus. Conversely, behavioral diversity can contribute to the stability and resilience of fish communities because it protects populations from local disturbances—both within a species and between different species.

articles.title: Light-matter hybrids form supersolid quantum state at room temperature
articles.dek: Researchers from the Faculty of Physics at the University of Warsaw, the Military University of Technology (Poland), IBM Research Zurich and the French National Centre for…
paragraphs: Researchers from the Faculty of Physics at the University of Warsaw, the Military University of Technology (Poland), IBM Research Zurich and the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) have observed a new quantum state of matter known as a supersolid in an exciton-polariton Bose-Einstein condensate. Remarkably, the phenomenon occurs not at temperatures close to absolute zero, but at room temperature. The results have been published in Science Advances .

At first glance, this seems impossible. A crystal is rigid and ordered, while a liquid flows. Yet quantum mechanics allows a state that combines both properties. The story begins with superfluidity—an extraordinary state of matter in which viscosity completely disappears. A superfluid can flow through the narrowest channels without resistance. If you dipped an oar into such a liquid, you would feel almost no drag until a critical velocity was exceeded, at which point quantum vortices would suddenly appear.

As early as the 1960s, physicists predicted that a superfluid could simultaneously develop a periodic crystal-like structure. The resulting phase, called a supersolid, retains the frictionless flow of a superfluid while exhibiting the spatial order of a crystal. For more than half a century, this remained a theoretical prediction. It was not until 2017 that supersolidity was experimentally observed in ultracold atomic Bose-Einstein condensates.

The TopoLight consortium chose a completely different route. Rather than using ultracold atoms, the researchers studied exciton polaritons —hybrid quasiparticles formed by the strong coupling between light and matter inside an optical microcavity. Although they exist for only a few picoseconds, this is sufficient for them to form a Bose–Einstein condensate and behave as a quantum superfluid.
The optical microcavity was filled with a specially designed liquid crystal and coated with an organic semiconductor. This combination enabled strong light-matter coupling at room temperature.

"Our liquid-crystal microcavities can operate even at temperatures approaching 60°C," says professor Wiktor Piecek from the Military University of Technology, whose group developed the liquid-crystal structures.

The transition into the supersolid phase is revealed by the appearance of regularly spaced bright fringes in the light emitted from the sample. These fringes indicate that the condensate has spontaneously formed a periodic density modulation—a hallmark of crystallization.
But the experiment revealed something even more remarkable.
With every laser pulse exciting the sample, the fringes appeared at a different position. Each time, the quantum system independently selected one of many equivalent configurations.

"This is a textbook example of spontaneous symmetry breaking," explains professor Guillaume Malpuech from Institut Pascal (CNRS). "Theory predicted that the supersolid could choose among several equivalent states, and that is exactly what we observed."

At the same time, the condensate also exhibited a persistent spin helix—a periodic modulation of the polarization of the emitted light. As a result, the researchers observed two distinct forms of order simultaneously: one in the polarization and another in the light intensity.
Performing the experiment proved far more challenging than anticipated.
The organic semiconductor gradually reacted with the liquid crystal, meaning that all measurements had to be completed within only a few hours after the sample was assembled.

"We had to plan the entire sequence of experiments in advance," recalls Dr. Marcin Muszyński, the paper's first author, now a postdoctoral researcher at The City College of New York. "Repeating a measurement meant fabricating an entirely new sample."

articles.title: Single-copy genes can be used as markers to distinguish between bacteria in the same family
articles.dek: The more than 100 bacterial species of the genus Vibrio are important in marine ecosystems because they contribute to the carbon cycle and other ecological processes, but…
paragraphs: The more than 100 bacterial species of the genus Vibrio are important in marine ecosystems because they contribute to the carbon cycle and other ecological processes, but they can also be significant pathogens for both humans (they can cause cholera) and animals (they can drastically reduce productivity in fish and crustacean farms [e. g. , prawns] or cause coral bleaching). Identifying and quantifying Vibrio species in marine and estuarine water samples is complex because identification errors may occur when using molecular methods that lack sufficient resolution.

"The genetic marker 16S rDNA is traditionally used for distinguishing between groups of bacteria that differ from one another. However, to distinguish between closely related bacteria that are highly similar, this marker is not so useful," explains researcher Alexandra García Flórez, author of a research study carried out at the EHU that demonstrates that single-copy genes can be used as markers for distinguishing between bacteria in the same family.

The resolution of the traditional 16S rDNA marker is not high enough to distinguish between highly similar species because its sequence is quite similar across closely related species. In addition, each bacterial cell can have more than one copy of this traditional marker, making it unsuitable for estimating abundances.

García's final-year project was aimed at improving the tools for identifying Vibrio species, using computational approaches based on molecular biology and microbial evolution. This work, now published in Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution is the result of a collaboration between EHU researchers Vladimir R. Kaberdin, of the Department of Immunology, Microbiology and Parasitology, and Peter B. Pearman, of the Department of Plant Biology and Ecology.

To find an alternative to the 16S rDNA marker, the research team selected "single-copy genes; that is, as the name suggests, each bacterium contains only one copy of this gene. Having one marker per bacterium helps us estimate the abundance of each species in a sample. In addition, these genes differ more between similar species, which means they enable the species to be distinguished more clearly," explains García.

By conducting a bioinformatics analysis of the sequences of the traditional 16S rDNA marker and the single-copy genes of 87 species of Vibrio, García was able to construct their evolutionary histories. After comparing them, the researchers concluded that "the 16S rDNA marker is not representative of the evolutionary history of the Vibrio species; it does not accurately reflect the evolutionary history shown by the single-copy genes."

The study demonstrated the validity of using single-copy genes as an alternative to the traditional marker genes in cases where a sufficiently high resolution cannot be achieved using the traditional marker. Once it has been confirmed that these genes "share a similar evolutionary history, the next step is to experimentally test them to see whether they can be used for analyzing the composition of Vibrios from a sample."

After a more detailed examination of the results of these analyses, the research team proposed some genes that could be used for an evolutionary study of the composition of microbial communities. García stated that, although the focus of this study was on Vibrios, "this analysis could be used for other types of bacteria."
Journal information: Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution

articles.title: Researchers develop method for single-cell DNA methylation analysis
articles.dek: Researchers have recently developed a standardized workflow for analyzing DNA methylation in individual cells.
paragraphs: Researchers have recently developed a standardized workflow for analyzing DNA methylation in individual cells. The protocol combines an improved laboratory procedure with an automated data analysis tool, making it easier to study differences between cells. Published in Nature Protocols , the study was led by researchers from the Institute of Health and Medical Technology at the Hefei Institutes of Physical Science of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

DNA methylation helps regulate gene activity and is involved in cell development and disease. Traditional sequencing measures average methylation levels across many cells, potentially masking differences between individual cells. Single-cell sequencing can reveal these differences, but the small amount of DNA in each cell makes sample preparation challenging.

To address the challenge, the researchers simplified several steps in the process. Cell preparation, DNA digestion and other reactions are carried out in the same microwell, reducing the need for repeated purification and helping prevent DNA loss. Molecular barcodes label individual samples, allowing 24 single-cell samples to be pooled for processing. This reduces reagent use and makes the process more efficient.
The researchers also developed an automated analysis tool, SingleCellMethPipe, which processes sequencing data, identifies methylation patterns and checks data quality.

To evaluate the method, the researchers analyzed 96 individual blood-forming stem and progenitor cells from a healthy donor and a patient with myelodysplastic syndrome, a disorder that affects the production of healthy blood cells.
Of these, 86 passed quality checks, giving a success rate of 89. 6%. The analysis identified DNA methylation differences between cell types and between the healthy and disease samples.
According to the researchers, the protocol provides a practical tool for studying how cells develop and how changes in DNA methylation are linked to blood disorders and cancer.

articles.title: Permanent Daylight Saving Time Could Send Millions of Kids to School in the Dark
articles.dek: Permanent daylight saving time could leave some states with roughly ten times as many dark school commutes, sharpening concerns about children’s safety and sleep.
paragraphs: Permanent daylight saving time could leave some states with roughly ten times as many dark school commutes, sharpening concerns about children’s safety and sleep.

Keeping daylight saving time through the winter would move sunrise an hour later on the clock, leaving children with fixed school schedules to make more trips in the dark. University of Washington researchers estimate that a nationwide shift would add at least 2 billion dark school commutes compared with the current system of switching between daylight saving time and standard time twice a year.

The U. S. House of Representatives passed a bill this past summer that would make daylight saving time (DST) permanent, ending the fall return to standard time. Nineteen states, including Washington, have already preapproved the change , which would take effect in those states if the bill is signed into law. The legislation is stalled in the U. S. Senate, with school start times a central issue because mornings would be darker from November through March.

The study, published October 29 in Current Biology , examined both school schedules and U. S. traffic collision data. The collision analysis found that a fatal crash involving a school-aged pedestrian was roughly twice as likely to occur during a dark morning as after sunrise.

Morning light also helps set the circadian clock, the body’s internal timing system, which helps regulate mood, sleep, and appetite. Without that light, the body has more difficulty regulating these functions.

“When we send kids to school in the dark, we are depriving them from an opportunity to get that morning daylight,” said lead author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a UW postdoctoral scholar in biology. “We were asking what’s the cost for these children. We wanted actual numbers, a real number of kids based on the geographic location of each school.”
Horacio de la Iglesia, UW professor of biology, discusses how permanent Daylight Saving Time will affect commutes for school children. Credit: Sarah McQuate/University of Washington

For 14 of the 19 states that had preapproved permanent DST, the researchers combined school start times, enrollment data, and latitude and longitude measurements. They calculated how many days each child would travel to school in the dark, then added those trips together to compare permanent DST with the current system.
All 14 states would see an increase. Washington would have almost 35 million additional dark trips to school, while Georgia would have the largest increase among the states studied, at 71 million.

Communities on the western edge of their time zones, such as Forks, Washington, would be particularly affected, as would those with early school start times. In Mississippi and Alabama, schools start before 8 a. m. on average. Each state would go from about 2 million dark school commutes under the current system to more than 20 million under permanent DST.

“Some districts probably never experience a dark commute under the current system, and, if this passes, suddenly they will wake up to this new reality that their kids are going to school in the dark,” Rodríguez Ferrante said. “Keep in mind that we used the actual start time listed for each school, and a lot of schools offer breakfast or other things before school, so the kids could be getting there even earlier.”
The nationwide estimate came from extrapolating the results from the 14 states to the rest of the country, with an assumption that makes the total likely conservative.
“For the estimation, we assumed students would be leaving home around 8 a. m. ,” Rodríguez Ferrante said. “That’s pretty late, so our calculation is likely an underestimation of the real number.”

“It’s called the ‘Sunshine Protection Act’ because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act,” said senior author Horacio de la Iglesia, a UW professor of biology. “These dark mornings will inequitably affect children who have to go to school at a certain time. It’s a very tangible metric that anybody from any state or socioeconomic background can relate to. Nobody wants their kids to go to school in the dark.”

articles.title: A Hidden Weakness in the Brain’s Defenses Could Help Explain Alzheimer’s Disease
articles.dek: A protein buildup damaged the brain’s protective barrier in animal experiments, pointing to a possible target for Alzheimer’s treatment.
paragraphs: A protein buildup damaged the brain’s protective barrier in animal experiments, pointing to a possible target for Alzheimer’s treatment.

Roughly one in five people carries at least one copy of APOE ε4, the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. Yet many people with the variant remain mentally sharp into their 80s without developing the disease. Understanding what protects some of them could help researchers find ways to protect others.

APOE ε4 carriers accumulate unusually high levels of a protein called fibronectin at the blood-brain barrier, a tightly packed layer of cells around brain blood vessels that helps remove toxic substances. Two years ago, Columbia University researchers discovered that a rare mutation in FN1, the gene that encodes fibronectin, limits this buildup and its damage, helping protect some carriers against Alzheimer’s. A drug that mimics that effect might offer similar protection.
The team’s latest study, published in Nature Aging , found that excess fibronectin can make the barrier leak in animal experiments and traced the damage to disrupted signals between cells.

“This new study takes us from a genetic clue to a disease mechanism,” says Caghan Kizil, the study’s corresponding author and professor of neurological sciences in the Department of Neurology and the Taub Institute for Research on Alzheimer’s Disease and the Aging Brain at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

“We knew that changes in fibronectin could protect against Alzheimer’s, but we didn’t know why excess fibronectin was harmful in the first place. This study gives us that detailed mechanism—and with it, ideas for how to reproduce that natural protection.”

In human brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid, the liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, high fibronectin levels were associated with inflamed astrocytes. These cells, also called astroglia, help maintain the blood-brain barrier. Genetic and epigenetic analyses, which examined genetic variation and gene regulation, also linked FN1 to vascular disease and changes in VEGFA, a growth factor needed to maintain healthy brain blood vessels.

“The convergence of these independent human datasets strengthens the case that fibronectin is part of the APOE ε4-related vascular disease process,” says Badri Vardarajan, associate professor of neurological science in the Department of Neurology, Gertrude H. Sergievsky Center, and Taub Institute, who collaborated on the discovery of the protective FN1 mutation.

To investigate how fibronectin affects the barrier, the researchers also used human stem-cell models, three-dimensional vascular cultures, and experiments in zebrafish and mice. Their methods included single-cell sequencing and spatial imaging. Across the systems they examined, the findings pointed to APOE ε4 increasing fibronectin and promoting its accumulation around brain blood vessels.

In mice carrying human APOE ε4, brain fibronectin levels were nearly twice those in mice carrying the normal human APOE version, APOE ε3. The higher levels coincided with evidence that the blood-brain barrier was leaking. That comparison alone could not establish whether fibronectin caused the damage, so the researchers performed a more targeted test. They increased human fibronectin specifically in astrocytes to determine whether excess protein in those cells was enough, by itself, to compromise the barrier.

“The animal experiments allowed us to move beyond association,” says co-first author Prabesh Bhattarai, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. “When we increased fibronectin in astroglia, the barrier became permeable. When we reduced fibronectin, barrier function improved.”

The researchers traced the damage to disrupted communication between cells. Excess fibronectin sends abnormal signals through integrins, proteins that sense a cell’s surroundings, and an enzyme called focal adhesion kinase. This disrupts a chain of growth factors called VEGF, HBEGF, and IGF1. These factors allow astrocytes and blood-vessel cells to communicate and work together to maintain the barrier.

“Single-cell analysis allowed us to examine this pathway in the different cells that maintain the brain’s blood vessels,” says co-first author Elanur Yilmaz, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. “We observed the same biological pattern across experimental models and human Alzheimer’s tissue, making the mechanism especially compelling.”

The human findings suggest that the same damaging processes likely occur in Alzheimer’s patients who carry APOE ε4, although the evidence that excess fibronectin itself can cause barrier leakage came from the animal experiments.

articles.title: A Rare Radioactive Element Reveals a Hidden Secret About the Heaviest Atoms
articles.dek: Using advanced laser spectroscopy on extremely rare radioactive material, researchers have uncovered new insights into the structure of heavy atomic nuclei.
paragraphs: Using advanced laser spectroscopy on extremely rare radioactive material, researchers have uncovered new insights into the structure of heavy atomic nuclei.

The nucleus of fermium-255 is far from spherical. Scientists have now determined its shape for the first time, finding that it is strongly elongated, much like a rugby ball. The high-precision measurements, published in Physical Review Letters , also correct earlier nuclear data and provide new evidence supporting theoretical models of the heaviest elements.

Fermium-255 contains 100 protons and 155 neutrons. In such heavy nuclei, the electrical repulsion between positively charged protons creates conditions that can lead to spontaneous fission, in which a nucleus splits into smaller fragments. Nuclear shape influences this process, making it a critical factor in predicting whether even heavier, potentially longer-lived elements can exist.

Rather than observing the nucleus directly, researchers studied its interactions with the electrons surrounding it. Electrons close to the nucleus are sensitive to its size, shape, and magnetic properties. These interactions produce extremely small differences in atomic energy levels that can be detected through precise laser measurements.

This phenomenon, known as hyperfine interaction, arises from the electromagnetic properties of the nucleus. A deformed nucleus interacts with the electric field of nearby electrons, while nuclear magnetism produces additional effects. Because fermium-255 has an odd number of neutrons, its nucleus also possesses a magnetic moment that contributes to the splitting of electronic energy levels.

Scientists at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU) first observed atomic energy levels in fermium more than 20 years ago. However, the technology available then could not resolve the fine details needed to determine its nuclear structure accurately. Some of the resulting nuclear data remained incomplete or inconsistent.

Fermium must be manufactured artificially, and obtaining enough atoms for an experiment requires an unusually complex production process. The researchers began with months of neutron irradiation of transuranium material at the High Flux Isotope Reactor at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (USA), producing einsteinium-254.

After initial experiments in the United States, the material traveled to Mainz (Germany) for processing and then to the Institute Laue-Langevin in France for additional neutron irradiation. This produced einsteinium-255, which decays into fermium-255. The material was subsequently returned to Mainz for spectroscopy experiments.

Einsteinium-255 has a half-life of approximately 40 days, allowing it to supply fermium-255 over several weeks. Through repeated chemical separations, scientists obtained individual samples containing tens of millions to about one billion fermium atoms. At JGU’s RISIKO separator, the samples were heated to approximately 1,000 degrees Celsius (1,832 degrees Fahrenheit) to release atoms for laser analysis. Specialized Ti laser systems excited and ionized the atoms, enabling researchers to resolve the hyperfine structure of two optical transitions despite the extremely small quantities available.

Researchers combined the experimental spectra with advanced atomic calculations performed at Jagiellonian University in Kraków, Poland, and the Helmholtz Institute Mainz (HIM). The analysis confirmed that the fermium-255 nucleus has a strongly prolate shape, meaning it is stretched along one axis. It also produced a magnetic dipole moment that differs from previously tabulated values, correcting earlier results that were inconsistent with physical expectations.

The measurements agree closely with modern nuclear theories developed by research groups in France and Germany. By providing more reliable information about nuclear deformation and magnetism, the findings strengthen models of nuclear fission and could improve predictions of the stability of superheavy elements that have yet to be discovered.

articles.title: Revolutionary Technology Could Transform How We Extract Lithium
articles.dek: A new breakthrough in lithium separation could help overcome major challenges in extracting this essential battery material.
paragraphs: A new breakthrough in lithium separation could help overcome major challenges in extracting this essential battery material.

A new technology developed at The University of Texas at Austin could make lithium extraction faster and more environmentally friendly by separating the valuable element from other dissolved substances with exceptional precision. The approach uses artificial channels so small they operate at the nanoscale, allowing lithium ions to pass through while blocking many competing ions.

Inspired by the molecular gateways found in living cells, the channels demonstrated two to five times greater lithium selectivity than other recently developed lithium transporters. Researchers report that the structures rank among the most selective lithium channels created to date, offering a potential alternative to conventional extraction methods.

Lithium is essential for batteries used in smartphones, electric vehicles, and electrical grids. It occurs in underground saltwater deposits known as brines, hard rock formations, and used batteries. However, these sources also contain elements such as sodium, potassium, magnesium, and calcium, whose ions can be difficult to separate from lithium. Existing extraction techniques often require considerable time and energy and can generate harmful waste.

“Lithium is in our phones, our cars and the power grid, but getting it out of the ground cleanly is still a hard problem,” said Manish Kumar, a professor in the Fariborz Maseeh Department of Civil, Architectural and Environmental Engineering and the McKetta Department of Chemical Engineering who is one of the leaders of the new research published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society . “Our goal is a process that is faster, cleaner and easier to run.”

The researchers designed tiny pores within membranes that mimic the selective transport pathways of biological cells. Their ability to distinguish lithium from other ions depends on two features working together: chemical groups positioned at the channel entrance and the tightly confined space inside. Interactions at the entrance, combined with the channel’s internal structure, favor lithium transport while restricting competing ions.

The study builds on earlier research into separating rare earth elements , which are important for technologies including wind turbine magnets and electronic displays. By extending the underlying design principles to lithium, the researchers are developing a broader approach to selectively recovering critical minerals.

“We now have a toolkit rather than a one-off result,” said Harekrushna Behera, a research scientist in Kumar’s lab. “By understanding how ions interact with the chemical groups at the channel entrance, we can work toward designing more selective channels for lithium and potentially other critical minerals.”

The next challenge is incorporating these highly selective channels into membranes large enough for practical lithium recovery. The team is exploring a recently developed material made from interconnected, cell-like layers that can be constructed using lipids or plastic-like polymers. Such membranes could eventually support continuous lithium separation without harsh chemical solvents.

Although the laboratory results demonstrate strong selectivity, the technology has not yet been validated for industrial extraction. Researchers still need to test its performance using real brines, where numerous dissolved salts coexist, and determine whether the channels can maintain their effectiveness at larger scales.

Beyond recovering lithium from natural deposits, the researchers envision using the same technology to reclaim the element from discarded batteries. Another possible application is improving the separators inside batteries themselves, although further development will be needed to establish whether these uses are practical.

articles.title: NASA Astronaut, STEM Creator Connect with Students for STEM Day
articles.dek: Students across the country will have the opportunity to connect directly with the International Space Station during a live, interactive in-flight call with NASA astronaut…
paragraphs: Students across the country will have the opportunity to connect directly with the International Space Station during a live, interactive in-flight call with NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Mark Rober STEM content creator and founder of ClassCrunchLabs Foundation. The event, hosted by NASA’s Office of STEM Engagement, celebrates National STEM Day by bringing real‑world science, engineering, and exploration into classrooms nationwide.
The Earth-to-space call will begin at 11 a. m. EST on Wednesday, Nov. 4, and will be available to watch on the agency’s flagship YouTube with additional engagement across Learn With NASA channels.

From aboard the space station, Menon will answer questions from students about living and working in microgravity, the path to becoming an astronaut, and the technologies that make human spaceflight possible. Rober, joining from California, will share how curiosity, creativity, and hands‑on problem‑solving shaped his career from NASA engineer to STEM creator.

During the downlink, students will see the space station in real time as Menon demonstrates how everyday activities, from eating to experimenting, change in microgravity. The downlink supports NASA’s broader effort to connect students with authentic STEM experiences to help build technical skills and introduce aerospace careers to students. National STEM Day is an opportunity to recognize the power of hands‑on learning and to inspire the next generation of scientists, technicians, engineers, and innovators who will carry NASA’s exploration goals forward.

This downlink also marks the launch of a new collaboration between NASA and the ClassCrunchLabs Foundation. Together, the organizations will work to broaden access to STEM learning experiences for students across the country by aligning NASA’s mission‑driven educational resources with CrunchLabs’ hands‑on engineering content. Through shared programming and outreach, the partnership aims to inspire more learners to engage with science, engineering, and problem‑solving skills that prepare them for future opportunities in the aerospace sector and beyond.
Educators and families are encouraged to tune in and celebrate National STEM Day with an inspiring conversation between a NASA astronaut in orbit and a STEM educator on Earth.

articles.title: Scientists Discover a Mysterious Comet 808 Million Miles From Earth
articles.dek: A distant comet following a millennia-long orbit could provide valuable insights into how future space missions identify and study these elusive objects.
paragraphs: A distant comet following a millennia-long orbit could provide valuable insights into how future space missions identify and study these elusive objects.

A space telescope built to study distant galaxies has discovered a previously unknown comet approximately 1. 3 billion kilometers (808 million miles) from Earth. The European Space Agency’s Euclid telescope captured the object in images taken between September 16 and 24, 2026, marking its first discovery of a new comet.

Now designated C/2026 S1 (Euclid), the comet follows an orbit that takes thousands of years to complete. Rather than traveling close to the plane where the planets orbit the Sun, it is currently positioned far above that plane, as viewed from the Sun. Its distance from Earth is comparable to the distance from the Sun to a point between Jupiter and Saturn.

Euclid was designed to map distant galaxies, not track comets and asteroids. Its observing strategy deliberately avoids the dust-rich band of sky along the Solar System’s plane, where scattered sunlight could interfere with sensitive measurements. The telescope also uses a “step-and-stare” approach that generally images each region only once, limiting opportunities to track moving objects over time.

Despite these obstacles, University of Helsinki researcher Mikko Pöntinen detected the comet using software he developed to identify moving Solar System objects in Euclid’s images. Working with the Euclid Consortium’s Solar System Objects Science Working Group, he found evidence of the object in five separate image sets.

“I was excited to see my software flag a ‘streak’ smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position, I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets [4]. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas.”

The fuzzy cloud surrounding the object was a sign of cometary activity. As ice in a comet warms and releases gas, it can carry dust into space, forming a diffuse envelope known as a coma. This distinguishes active comets from most asteroids, which typically lack such visible clouds.

After finding no matching object in existing comet and asteroid catalogs, Pöntinen reported the observations to the International Astronomical Union’s Minor Planet Center (MPC). The report prompted follow-up observations by ground-based astronomers, and the MPC officially confirmed the discovery on October 8, 2026.

“Very few comets are expected to be discovered by Euclid so it was a happy coincidence that the combination of the comet’s orbit and Euclid’s scanning over those days captured the object in multiple images,” said Bruno Altieri, Euclid Archive Scientist and a member of the discovery team.

Identifying moving objects is necessary for Euclid’s primary science mission because comet trails and other unwanted light can interfere with precise measurements of distant galaxies. The same detection techniques could also help astronomers discover comets while they are still relatively far from the Sun.

The rapid identification and confirmation of C/2026 S1 (Euclid) provides a practical test of how such discoveries could support ESA’s future Comet Interceptor mission. Although this particular comet is not a suitable target, the process demonstrates how Euclid’s observations could help scientists identify and assess other candidates.

“While this particular comet is not a suitable candidate for Comet Interceptor, the process of discovery and alert gives us a real test case for how our two mission teams will coordinate in the future. And we are, of course, happy to have discovered a previously unknown comet for the Solar System community to follow-up on,” said Valeria Pettorino, Euclid Project Scientist.

articles.title: Meta’s $25B fine left out accountability for harm from the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal
articles.dek: “The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate,” wrote a New Mexico judge who ordered tech giant Meta to pay one of the largest data privacy case penalties in American…
paragraphs: “The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate,” wrote a New Mexico judge who ordered tech giant Meta to pay one of the largest data privacy case penalties in American history. The US$25 billion fine came in a case about how Trump campaign firm Cambridge Analytica deceptively used data from Facebook users without their permission to create psychographic profiles to target voters in the lead-up to the 2016 presidential election.

But the New Mexico penalty was for statements Facebook made that deceived users about data privacy and its response to Cambridge Analytica – not for the harm caused by how the harvested data was used. Those harms are alleged to include exploiting psychological vulnerabilities, targeting people’s fears and discouraging them from voting .

I’m a political communication scholar who studies propaganda, surveillance and information warfare . My research helped expose the Cambridge Analytica scandal through U. K. newspaper The Guardian’s reporting on whistelblower accounts and the evidence I uncovered. That evidence was submitted to parliamentary and congressional investigations . I have followed the unfolding legal cases closely.

My takeaway from a decade of litigation is that Facebook has been penalized for misleading users and regulators about its data practices and its response to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. But I would contend that the company has largely escaped accountability for the underlying political exploitation of that data.
The failure to bring cases around harms may be partly due to earlier failures to fully investigate the data misuse.

The Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election encompassed Cambridge Analytica. However, the committee stated in its final report that it “was unable to obtain the corporate communications of Cambridge Analytica or its parent company SCL Group, which had already been seized by U. K. authorities.”

The relevant U. K. authorities, the Information Commissioner’s Office, which governs data protection and took possession of Cambridge Analytica’s servers, told me in response to my 2021 Freedom of Information Act request that the Senate committee staff made initial inquiries to the office but appear not to have followed up with a formal request, “so no information sharing has taken place.” Without a formal request, the Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation lacked important data.

At the same time, the U. K. investigations of Cambridge Analytica’s use of personal data to manipulate voting behavior focused on the referendum of British voters over whether to leave the E. U. , not events in the U. S.

A 2020 documentary film I advised as a researcher, “ People You May Know ,” raised questions about Cambridge Analytica’s work with an app marketed to American churches, called Gloo, that used Cambridge Analytica’s Facebook data-derived psychographic profiling in their communities. Evidence in the New Mexico case reinvigorates these questions about the full extent of the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

The judge in the case ruled Facebook knew that its own processes for investigating whether apps misused personal data were inadequate and that it could not enforce deletion of the data. The judge also concluded the company failed to notify users about thousands of applications associated with data misuse . Meta said it would appeal the decision.

Meta responded to a request for comment with the company’s official statement about the New Mexico ruling, arguing the case “seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.” Meta did not address the issue of its own role in the data privacy violations committed by Cambridge Analytica.
Meta is also trying to close the door on further claims before they are litigated.

In August 2026, on the eve of a child-safety trial in federal court in Oakland, California, Meta settled with a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general for roughly $17 billion. The agreement includes 47 states, the District of Columbia and two U. S. territories. Folded into that deal was an allocation of $459. 3 million to settle Cambridge Analytica-related claims held by participating states.

The participating attorneys general agreed, to the extent of their authority, to “fully, finally, and forever” release Meta from “any and all Claims, whether known or unknown, whether accrued or unaccrued.” By expressly encompassing “unknown” and “unaccrued” claims, the agreement reached beyond what investigators had already uncovered. Participating states accepted payment to give up claims arising from Meta’s conduct even if they did not yet know those claims existed.
A decade-old matter - Facebook’s role in the Cambridge Analytica scandal - was quietly brushed under the rug in an unrelated lawsuit about harm to teens.

From the 2019 Federal Trade Commission order to the 2022 class action settlement to August 2026’s multistate deal , settlements and releases have meant the company paid a relatively small price for its deception while not having the harms from the data exploitation adjudicated. Ultimately, the biggest privacy judgment in American history stands as a measure of the cover-up, not the alleged crime.

Other scholars and I regularly call attention to the lack of comprehensive U. S. privacy legislation , but there remain other legal pathways to pursue the harms Cambridge Analytica wrought. States like New Mexico can continue the fight, and Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who brought the case, promised, “ We’re just getting started .”

Dissenting from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, then-Commissioner Rohit Chopra criticized the failure to consider “ Facebook’s unjust enrichment .” He said “the company’s potential exposure is likely far greater” than the $5 billion imposed by the FTC settlement.

The question remains what exactly Facebook gained from enabling Cambridge Analytica’s abuses. Authorities could also investigate harmful data use for any other apps Facebook may have failed to fully assess, including any associated with Cambridge Analytica’s projects.

If the deception about Cambridge Analytica is worth $25 billion, I believe the public is entitled to know what the underlying harms to them are worth. New Mexico opted out of the 2026 multistate settlement and proved that a state willing to go to trial against Meta can win.

The next task, in my view, is to investigate fully and, where legal claims remain available, pursue accountability for harms resulting from the data exploitation. Otherwise, Cambridge Analytica will remain at the heart of the most consequential privacy scandal in American history, whose full harms have not been tested in court.

articles.title: Pediatric palliative care addresses the unique needs of seriously ill children and their families
articles.dek: Pediatric medicine generally entails caring for patients at the beginning of their lives – performing newborn checkups, treating childhood illnesses and supporting…
paragraphs: Pediatric medicine generally entails caring for patients at the beginning of their lives – performing newborn checkups, treating childhood illnesses and supporting adolescents in their health as they move toward adulthood.
So people are often surprised to hear about specialists like us who work in pediatric palliative care , helping children facing serious illness who may be nearing the end of their lives.

This approach to care focuses on relieving suffering and addressing quality of life for children and families facing complex, life-limiting medical conditions. We also work to ensure that every family who needs it has access to this care, because right now, these programs aren’t available to most families globally who need them.
Pediatric palliative care is an approach that emerged out of the adult hospice and palliative care movement in the 1990s to early 2000s as a distinct discipline.

Globally, an estimated 7 million children die annually . Children with life-threatening health conditions often live longer between the time of diagnosis and death than adults. They benefit from approaches to care that consider the needs of their caregivers and family members .

Pediatric palliative care is provided by a team of professionals, including physicians, nurses, social workers, child life specialists, chaplains and other allied health professionals who take a comprehensive approach to a child’s care as they live with serious illness and ultimately approach the end of their life. The goal of this care is to support families in making every day as good as it possibly can be, regardless of whether or not a child’s life remaining is short. At the heart of this approach is the belief that each child has a right to holistic, empathetic care during illness and throughout end of their life that considers their unique social, cultural, physical and spiritual needs.

For example, an infant who is diagnosed with a rare genetic disorder that affects vital organ function and shortens life expectancy may need to be in and out of the hospital to manage acute illnesses and complex symptoms, such as pain and difficulty breathing. In turn, her parents may need help with deciding which treatments will be most helpful or may cause more suffering than benefit.

A palliative care team works with patients and caregivers to formulate a plan that ensures this baby gets care that affords her opportunities to experience as many happy moments as possible. This can improve the lived experience of this child and her parents.

Children and families who have benefited from pediatric palliative care describe these services as the supportive lifeline that helped them to navigate the complexities of diagnosis, life with serious illness and, ultimately, death and bereavement.

Over the past 20 years, there has been growing evidence suggesting the benefits of this approach. Children who receive care from pediatric palliative care specialists have less pain, nausea and other distressing symptoms that can affect their day-to-day function and overall quality of life.

Research also shows that children admitted to intensive care settings for managing life-threatening illness are more likely to receive care that aligns with their goals. When a palliative care specialist is consulted, patients are less likely to opt for life-sustaining therapies that would not change their long-term prognosis.

The U. S. is on the global forefront of pediatric palliative care: Nearly 80% of U. S. children’s hospitals have formal, interdisciplinary programs to provide this specialized care. But access to services in a clinic setting or at home is less consistent. Not every hospital-based palliative care program is connected to outpatient or home-based services, creating gaps for patients and families who need to access this supportive care between hospitalizations.

Generally, palliative care in the U. S. is more readily available in urban settings and at academic medical centers than in rural areas and community hospitals. These differences are most pronounced in rural states and the Southeast , a region of the country that has historically had health disparities across racial and socioeconomic differences . It can be difficult for children in these places to access patient-centered, interdisciplinary supportive services.

Outside the U. S. , pediatric palliative care can be even more difficult to access. Though it’s hard to measure , estimates suggest that more than 21 million children worldwide would benefit from a pediatric palliative care approach.

More than half of the world’s population live in countries where the availability of any palliative care is defined as either emerging or progressing, according to the World Health Organization. Only 14% of countries – 28 total – are considered to have advanced levels of palliative care development. The numbers are fairly similar for pediatrics, with one study identifying only 11 countries as reaching the highest level of pediatric palliative care development.

As many as 97% of children in need of this approach live in low- and middle-income countries . Children in these countries have less access to medical diagnostic and therapeutic interventions and are often diagnosed at later stages of illness with less access to curative therapy.

The types of pediatric serious illnesses seen in the developing world are also very different from the landscape in the U. S. The greatest need for pediatric palliative care in developing nations – about 30% of cases – is in children with HIV . Among other children needing palliative care , about 18% are living with complications from prematurity, roughly 16% suffer from congenital malformations, and about 16% are dealing with injuries leading to severe neurologic impairment.

In contrast to many high-income settings, children with malignant diseases such as leukemias and solid tumors represent a relatively small proportion – about 4% – of patients who would benefit from a palliative care approach. In these regions, the predominant ailments are HIV/AIDS, premature birth and birth trauma, congenital anomalies and injuries.

In low- and middle-income countries, essential medications like morphine, used for controlling pain and other symptoms, often aren’t available . In addition, healthcare workers often haven’t been trained in foundational principles of palliative care .
On top of that, many of these countries don’t have the political infrastructure to provide basic healthcare , much less facilitate developing a comprehensive palliative care program for children.

The good news is that there are existing models for countries that are starting from scratch to build upon. And there’s room for innovation. Established community partnerships and technologies can be leveraged in new ways – for instance, using online learning and video conferencing to help train healthcare workers and build relationships.

We believe pediatric palliative care is the heart of what healthcare should be when a child faces a serious, life-limiting illness, regardless of where they live in the world. Because even when medicine cannot cure, it can always heal and comfort.
