articles.title: Menopause can quietly weaken bones – here’s what research reveals about protecting them
articles.dek: A skeleton hanging on a door or standing in your neighbor’s yard for Halloween looks like a finished structure. But the skeleton inside a living body is constantly changing.
paragraphs: A skeleton hanging on a door or standing in your neighbor’s yard for Halloween looks like a finished structure. But the skeleton inside a living body is constantly changing. Around menopause, those changes can tip toward bone loss, often without pain or another obvious warning.

I am a skeletal biology researcher at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. My work examines how hormonal and metabolic signals influence bone renewal. In my assessment, the quiet nature of bone loss makes menopause an important time to bring skeletal health into the conversation.

Bone loss can start accelerating before the final menstrual period. Natural menopause is confirmed only after 12 consecutive months without a period , when there is no other explanation. Bone loss can therefore accelerate before someone knows that their last period was their final one.

Bones are living tissues that continually renew themselves . During this process, called remodeling, cells known as osteoclasts remove old bone while other cells – osteoblasts – build its replacement. Estrogen helps regulate this renewal. As estrogen levels decline around menopause, removal can outpace replacement, contributing to bone loss and osteoporosis , a condition in which bones become more fragile and porous.
Osteoporosis can affect women and men. It becomes more common with age but can also occur in younger people. A person often has no noticeable symptoms until a fracture occurs.

The timing is revealing. An analysis of 862 participants in the Study of Women’s Health Across the Nation , a long-term U. S. study of women in midlife, tracked changes in bone density in relation to their final menstrual period. On average, loss at the lower spine and near the hip was fastest from about one year before that period through two years afterward. It then slowed rather than stopped.

These findings do not mean that everyone experiences the same amount of bone loss or develops osteoporosis. They show why the menopausal transition itself deserves attention, rather than treating bone loss as a concern only for older women.

To assess a person’s risk of breaking a bone, clinicians consider factors such as low body weight, smoking, excessive alcohol use and whether a patient’s parent experienced a hip fracture. A bone density scan measures bone mineral density and helps assess fracture risk. It provides useful information alongside medical history and other risk factors.

The U. S. Preventive Services Task Force, an independent panel of experts in preventive care, recommends screening for osteoporosis in women age 65 and older. It also recommends screening younger postmenopausal women when their health history and other risk factors indicate a higher chance of a fracture. This does not mean every woman needs a scan as soon as her periods change.

These recommendations address routine screening. People who already have osteoporosis, have broken a bone after a minor fall or have a disease or take medicines that cause bone loss need evaluation tailored to their circumstances.

A U. K. trial illustrates how identifying people at high risk and recommending treatment can help . More than 12,000 women age 70 to 85 received either usual care or screening, followed by treatment recommendations for those at high risk. Over five years, women in the screening group were less likely to break a hip. However, when the researchers considered osteoporosis-related fractures across different parts of the body together, they did not find a statistically significant reduction. The findings support screening linked to treatment in older women, but do not tell us when screening should begin during the menopausal transition.

Bones respond to the forces placed on them. Weight-bearing activities such as walking and stair climbing make bones support the body’s weight. Resistance exercises using weights, bands or body weight create additional forces on bones as muscles pull against them. Balance training, such as tai chi and exercises that practice shifting weight from one foot to the other, can improve stability and help prevent falls. Activity for bone health therefore involves more than one kind of movement.

An Australian trial published in 2018 tested whether supervised heavy resistance exercises and impact movements could improve bone density and physical function in postmenopausal women with low bone mass. After eight months, participants in that program had better results than those following a less intensive home exercise program. The women were carefully screened, and the training was closely supervised.

These improvements are encouraging, but improved bone density is not the same outcome as fewer broken bones: The trial did not establish whether its program reduced fractures. People with osteoporosis, previous fractures or physical limitations may need guidance on appropriate movements and loads. Building muscle strength and balance can support mobility as well as bone health. Choosing suitable exercise depends on a person’s own circumstances.

Nutrition contributes in a different way. Calcium supplies mineral that helps give bones their strength , while vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium . Adequate protein also forms part of a balanced diet. Calcium-rich foods include dairy products, fortified alternatives, canned sardines or salmon with edible bones, and vegetables such as bok choy and broccoli.

Calcium or vitamin D supplements may help when a person’s intake is insufficient or they have a deficiency that needs treatment. They do not replace osteoporosis medicines when those are needed. Nutrition and treatment work together.

Systemic menopausal hormone therapy — treatment that delivers hormones throughout the body — can relieve bothersome hot flashes and night sweats and help prevent bone loss and fractures. Its benefits and risks depend on age, time since menopause, medical history and the treatment used.

For women younger than 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset who have no medical reasons to avoid it, the balance of benefits and risks from menopausal hormone therapy is generally favorable for treating troublesome symptoms and preventing bone loss. This does not mean hormone therapy is suitable for everyone. Patients and clinicians should discuss their symptoms, bone health and individual risks, and revisit the decision over time.

Other osteoporosis medicines can slow bone breakdown or stimulate bone formation. Clinicians also consider other medical conditions and medicines that can weaken bones , including hormonal disorders, digestive conditions and long-term glucocorticoid treatment. Menopause may be only part of the explanation.

One example is primary hyperparathyroidism , in which one or more parathyroid glands in the neck produce too much parathyroid hormone. This can raise blood calcium and weaken bones. Identifying it can change the care plan. It illustrates why investigating the cause of bone loss matters, rather than simply attributing it to aging.

Advice about scans and treatment assumes people can obtain them. Looking beyond individual choices shows how access to care can shape the options available. One example comes from a 2025 audit of 22 Asia-Pacific countries and regions . It documented substantial differences in access to osteoporosis care. Bone density scan waits ranged from the same day to nearly a year, and gaps in coverage for medicines limited the affordability of treatment. The regional audit concerns osteoporosis broadly, not only menopause.
In other words, making prevention possible requires both public awareness and health systems that make scans, follow-up care and treatment accessible and affordable.

Menopause offers an opportunity to ask about the skeleton while a person still feels well. The answer may involve a risk assessment, suitable activity, nutritional changes or medical treatment. A bone health conversation can begin long before a fracture starts it.

Priya Bhardwaj is employed by Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. She serves on the Endocrine Society’s Bone and Mineral Special Interest Group steering committee and ASBMR Women in Bone and Mineral SIG Commitee.

articles.title: As it gets harder to figure out what to eat, some Americans are turning to religion for answers
articles.dek: It’s getting harder and harder to figure out what to eat. A scroll through social media raises many questions. Why is food so expensive? Am I getting enough protein?
paragraphs: It’s getting harder and harder to figure out what to eat. A scroll through social media raises many questions. Why is food so expensive? Am I getting enough protein? What about fiber? Do I need supplements? Should I be making all my bread at home? What foods were recalled this week?
These questions make trips to the grocery store and mealtime decisions more difficult. For centuries, some people have turned to their religious texts and traditions for answers.
In “ Born Again Bodies ,” religious studies scholar R. Marie Griffith traces how Protestant Christian ideas on faith and the body shaped the development of American diet and fitness culture.

Through my decade of ethnographic research on religious food movements, I have found that many Americans are still turning to religion as they decide what to eat. I analyzed four religious alternative food movements in my 2025 book, “ Free-Range Religion .” I argue there that these movements aren’t just changing what they eat; they are working to reshape the American food system from the ground up.

Two of the sites I studied were Jewish farms that were providing experiential education opportunities for the local Jewish community. It was part of their larger mission to reconnect Jews to the land and to the agrarian roots of Judaism. They often point out that the ancient Israelites were an agrarian people and that many Jewish laws, values and holidays were shaped by that context.

At the Isabella Freedman Jewish Retreat Center in Falls Village, Connecticut, I worked alongside young Jewish adults participating in a three-month program, the Adamah Farm Fellowship , as they planted, harvested and prepared produce for their weekly community supported agriculture program. The fellows begin their days with a morning prayer session and take time away from their work on the farm to celebrate Shabbat together. The fellows also attend classes where they learn about the biblical laws and ethical concepts related to agriculture, alongside scientific research on sustainable agriculture.

I conducted my fieldwork during a “shmita” year, a year of rest for the land . Just as the Hebrew Bible instructed Jews to work for six days and rest on Shabbat, the seventh day, they were also instructed to work their land for six years and then let it rest in the seventh year, the shmita year.

Farms took different approaches to the “shmita” year: The Adamah Farm Fellows kept their fields in production and started a community garden to mark their observance of the “shmita” year. At the Pearlstone center in Reisterstown, Maryland, the farmers replaced their usual rows of vegetables with cover crops that would enrich the soil during its year of rest. They also canceled their community supported agriculture program and focused their educational programs on the Jewish texts and traditions of “shmita” and the importance of rest for all beings.

Another group I studied were followers of the Hallelujah Diet, a plant-based diet rooted in the biblical story of the Garden of Eden. In “ The Hallelujah Diet ,” first published in 2006, the Rev. George Malkmus determined that the ideal food system was laid out in the first chapter of the Book of Genesis, where God instructs humans to eat plants, fruits and seeds . In the Garden of Eden, Adam and Eve would not have had access to cooked food, so the Hallelujah Diet also prioritizes the consumption of raw, uncooked vegan foods.

I attended a Hallelujah Diet health retreat in Lake Lure, North Carolina, in 2015 with nine followers of the Hallelujah Diet. This was a small subset of Hallelujah dieters. In the summer of 2013, I attended a talk by George Malkmus in Charlotte, North Carolina, along with hundreds of Hallelujah dieters.

Religion scholar Annie Blazer found that followers of the Hallelujah Diet tend to believe that it will cure their ailments and help them lead long and healthy lives. I found that the reality is a bit more complicated.

The retreat guests were adopting the diet in the hope that it would help them address medical issues, but they were not solely relying on the diet to heal them. The retreat guests were also seeing healthcare professionals and taking medications, recovering from or scheduling surgeries, and visiting physical therapists.

The fourth site I studied was Baldwin Beef , a family-owned cattle farm that produced 100% grass-fed beef in Yanceyville, North Carolina. The Baldwins are Christian and raise their cows in line with their understanding that, according to the Bible, cows are meant to live on pasture and eat grass.

This differs from the more common practice in the United States of moving cattle to feedlots for their final months and feeding them grain . The Baldwins also collaborated with a smaller-scale halal slaughterhouse to ensure that their cows experienced less stress in their final moments.

Christians and many other religious Americans have been wrestling with their relationship with animals and the ethics of eating meat since the 19th century. Many contemporary religious and nonreligious movements are reconsidering current animal welfare practices. In some cases, this means advocacy for vegetarianism or veganism and in others it means working to address issues in animal agriculture.

I use the term “free-range religion” in my book’s title for a reason: Americans belong to many communities at once, including religious communities, and the boundaries between communities are often porous.
For example, on the surface, the Hallelujah Diet book appears to be a Christian diet, written by a reverend. But I found that the reality was more complicated.

At the Hallelujah Diet health retreat I attended, all the participants were Christian – except for me, I’m Jewish – but the leaders of the retreat were Messianic Jews , who identify as Jews but believe Jesus was the Messiah. During our time at the retreat, we encountered a number of theological differences within our group, but our hosts encouraged us to remain focused on our shared interest in improving our bodily health.

In our educational sessions, medical doctors were cited as sources alongside biblical prophets, reflecting the range of authorities Hallelujah dieters recognize. The retreat participants similarly incorporated an array of practices into their daily lives, including yoga, meditation and the use of essential oils.
They saw some of these practices as part of their spiritual practice, while others were curtained off as “new age” and were seen as practices they engaged in outside of their Christianity.

As British anthropologist Mary Douglas demonstrated many decades ago in “ Purity and Danger ,” religion plays a central role in food choices as communities make determinations about what is considered clean and unclean. For many religious communities, food rules bring them together through shared values and identities but also separate them from others.

That is certainly happening today. Many communities still use food as a way to establish boundaries for membership. Jewish communities, for example, regularly establish rules around what people can bring to events to preserve the kosher status of synagogue kitchens. The kosher laws include restrictions on the types of meat that can be consumed and prohibits mixing meat and dairy in the same meal, so keeping a kitchen kosher requires communal adherence to these rules.

But these food decisions are also bringing religious and nonreligious people together in interesting ways and creating new collaborations in their efforts to transform the food system. The Jewish farmers from Adamah and Pearlstone are now part of a large umbrella organization, also called Adamah , that engages in interfaith climate advocacy work at national and international levels.

All of the groups I studied identified a concern regarding the food system. For the Jewish farmers, it was that Jews had become disconnected from food production. For the Hallelujah dieters, it was a concern that people were not eating the diet that they believed humans were created by God to eat in the Garden of Eden. For the Baldwin family, it was a concern that modern beef production did not align with biblical descriptions of cattle grazing on green pastures.

articles.title: Nearly 7 in 10 professors report being bullied, often by students over grades
articles.dek: Faculty and university staff members report being bullied in two ways: by their colleagues and supervisors, and by their students over grades , according to an international…
paragraphs: Faculty and university staff members report being bullied in two ways: by their colleagues and supervisors, and by their students over grades , according to an international study I conducted with colleagues Zahra Moradi and Deborah Circo .

Researchers define workplace bullying as harmful acts of mistreatment between people that go beyond incivility and cross the line to intentionally cause harm. In other words, it’s behavior any reasonable person would know isn’t OK.
Junior faculty and staff faced more workplace bullying from peers. Faculty members and staff who are Black, Indigenous or people of color were targeted more frequently.

Senior faculty were more likely than younger educators to report being bullied by students over grades. Although bullying usually runs down the chain of power – for example, from a boss to an employee – grade bullying flips that. Researchers call it contrapower harassment – when someone with less formal power targets someone with more.
More than 30% of adult workers in the U. S. and Canada experience bullying, harassment and sexual abuse in the workplace at any given time, harming both individuals and organizations .

That rate is more than double in academia, where bullying rates are as high as 68% at some institutions, far exceeding those in general workplaces and aligning with high-stress fields like emergency services , according to our peer-reviewed findings published in the October 2026 Journal of Multidisciplinary Research and Practice.
Academic bullying undermines both the well-being of staff and faculty and the integrity of higher education institutions.

Thirty percent of our survey respondents reported that students pressured them for a better grade. Students’ tactics included threatening grade appeals, malicious complaints, negative online reviews, emotional manipulation and intimidation. Women and minority faculty are particularly affected. Over time, the bullying creates a toxic environment that damages relationships between faculty and students and hurts the quality of education for everyone.

Such pressure could result in mental health issues like anxiety and depression, decreased job satisfaction and reduced productivity. These dynamics not only affect individual faculty members but can also lead to long-term damage to the reputation of institutions and negatively impact students’ educational experiences.
We surveyed 189 faculty and staff at colleges and universities in Canada, the U. S. and U. K.
Anonymous respondents reported how often they’d faced 22 common forms of mistreatment from colleagues and supervisors. A separate set of questions asked about pressure from students over grades.
The most common issues related to colleagues weren’t shouting or threats. They were easier to dismiss: unmanageable workloads, withheld information and impossible deadlines.
Pressure from students over grades was reported more frequently than bullying from colleagues.
Gaps remain in understanding the root causes of bullying of faculty.

Studies that follow the same faculty over several years could show how grade bullying builds over time, and whether it pushes people to leave or lose trust in their institutions. One likely pattern is that grade bullying escalates when it works, wearing faculty down until they either give in or leave their jobs.
Researchers need to test what actually works to stop bullying, and whether those fixes hold up at different kinds of colleges and universities.
Bigger studies would help. So would sitting down with faculty and hearing their experiences in their own words to add context that a survey can’t capture.
Future research could also explore interventions to mitigate bullying and measure their effectiveness across diverse educational contexts.

Bullying at work is a form of violence. The harm is psychological rather than physical, but it’s real. Change starts with higher standards of conduct for everyone, from first-year students to senior administrators and leaders committed to enforcing respectful rules.

articles.title: Breakthrough Cancer Treatment Wipes Out Deadly Brain Tumors in Every Mouse Tested
articles.dek: A new approach to engineering immune cells has shown remarkable success against a deadly childhood brain cancer in mice.
paragraphs: A new approach to engineering immune cells has shown remarkable success against a deadly childhood brain cancer in mice.

An experimental immune cell therapy has completely eliminated an aggressive childhood brain cancer in mice, succeeding where conventional treatments have struggled. Developed by scientists at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), the approach uses genetically engineered CAR-T cells that activate their cancer-fighting receptors only after entering the brain.

The treatment, called B-SYNC, cleared tumors in every mouse tested across two models of diffuse midline glioma (DMG). It also provided lasting protection, with treated mice rejecting a second introduction of cancer cells nearly seven weeks later. Researchers are now preparing for human clinical trials that could begin as early as April 2027.

DMG is particularly difficult to treat because it infiltrates healthy brain tissue, often growing within the brainstem. This region regulates essential functions such as breathing, heart rate, and swallowing, making surgical removal extremely dangerous or impossible. Children diagnosed with the disease almost always die within a year.

CAR-T therapy offers a different strategy. It involves modifying immune T cells to recognize specific proteins on cancer cells and attack them. Although this approach has transformed treatment for certain blood cancers, conventional CAR-T therapies have not successfully controlled brain tumors such as DMG.

“It’s been a struggle to make CAR-T cells that overcome DMG without causing unacceptable side effects,” said Hideho Okada, MD, PhD, a UCSF professor of Neurological Surgery and co-corresponding author of the study, published October 28 in Science Translational Medicine . “By limiting B-SYNC’s CAR expression to when and where it matters — in the brain — we saw consistent, total shutdown of DMG tumors in the lab.”

B-SYNC uses a molecular switch that responds to brevican, a protein widely distributed throughout the brain. The researchers equipped T cells with a synthetic sensor called synNotch that detects brevican and triggers the production of cancer-targeting chimeric antigen receptors (CARs).

Once activated, these receptors allow the T cells to attack cells carrying either of two proteins, EphA2 or IL13Rα2, which are found on many brain tumor cells. Because brevican controls when the receptors are produced, the therapy is designed to restrict its tumor-targeting activity to the brain rather than allowing the engineered receptors to remain active throughout the body.

The technology builds on an earlier UCSF treatment called E-SYNC, developed by Okada and Wendell Lim, PhD, a professor of Cellular and Molecular Pharmacology. Announced in 2021, E-SYNC used synNotch to recognize EGFRvIII, a mutant protein associated with glioblastoma, before activating receptors targeting EphA2 and IL13Rα2. However, only about 20% of glioblastoma patients have tumors carrying EGFRvIII, and cancer cells can lose this marker as treatment eliminates those that express it.

Replacing EGFRvIII with brevican gave the researchers a more broadly available activation signal within the brain. Since DMG cells also frequently express EphA2 and IL13Rα2, the redesigned system could potentially target this childhood cancer without depending on a mutation present in only a subset of tumors.

To investigate the treatment, UCSF postdoctoral researcher Senthilnath Lakshmanachetty, PhD, administered B-SYNC CAR-T cells intravenously (IV) to mice implanted with human DMG cells. Some of the engineered cells entered the brain, activated their receptors, and attacked the tumors.

Tests showed that B-SYNC cells circulating elsewhere, including in the blood and spleen, did not produce the cancer-targeting receptors. This confirmed that their activation was restricted to the intended tissue, “just as we designed it,” Lakshmanachetty said.

The researchers next delivered the cells directly into the brain’s fluid-filled ventricles through an intracerebroventricular (ICV) injection. This method produced stronger results, completely clearing tumors in every treated mouse across two human DMG models. Conventional CAR-T cells, tested for comparison, again failed to control the cancer.

The scientists also investigated whether the modified immune cells could remain functional after the original tumors disappeared. Nearly seven weeks after treatment, they introduced another round of DMG cells into the mice. Every animal previously treated with B-SYNC rejected the new cancer cells.

articles.title: Too Much Exercise Could Change Your Brain Chemistry in Unexpected Ways
articles.dek: Two days after an exercise test, mice subjected to weeks of grueling training still had elevated dopamine levels in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory and…
paragraphs: Two days after an exercise test, mice subjected to weeks of grueling training still had elevated dopamine levels in the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory and emotional regulation. The findings suggest that excessive exercise without adequate recovery can produce lasting changes in brain chemistry.

The study, published in the journal Neuroscience , was conducted by researchers in Brazil. Because dopamine helps regulate motivation and alertness, the results raise questions about whether similar disruptions could contribute to sleep problems, anxiety, and persistent fatigue in overtrained athletes. However, these possible effects have not been demonstrated in humans.

To investigate how different levels of physical exertion affect the brain, the researchers compared mice subjected to two exercise protocols. One group completed a single treadmill session until exhaustion. The other underwent eight weeks of progressively more demanding training designed to simulate the physical strain associated with overtraining syndrome.

During the final week, the heavily trained mice exercised twice daily, with just four hours between sessions. Researchers then examined the animals’ hippocampi, measuring dopamine, serotonin, and proteins involved in neurotransmitter production and regulation.

The mice that completed a single exhausting run showed a rise in dopamine shortly afterward. In contrast, the chronically trained animals had elevated dopamine levels even 48 hours after their performance test, during a period intended for recovery. Levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme essential for dopamine synthesis, also remained elevated.

Dopamine is involved in several functions, including motivation, reward processing, and wakefulness. Its presence is not inherently harmful, but changes in its regulation could affect brain activity during periods when the body would normally be recovering.

Interestingly, the researchers found no significant changes in serotonin levels. Serotonin has long been investigated as a possible contributor to exercise-related fatigue, but these results suggest that the neurochemical effects of excessive training cannot be explained by serotonin alone.

“Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain,” said Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study’s first author. He conducted the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP), with support from FAPESP.

Overtraining syndrome occurs when prolonged physical demands exceed the body’s ability to recover, potentially causing declining athletic performance, chronic fatigue, muscle pain, loss of appetite, increased injuries, and changes in immune and metabolic function. Researchers suspect that changes in brain signaling may also contribute to some symptoms.

Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, suggested that similar dopamine disturbances in humans might help explain connections between excessive training and sleep disorders. However, the researchers did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness in the mice, so the findings cannot establish a connection between the observed chemical changes and those symptoms.

The research team is now participating in an international project to identify which biological systems first begin to show abnormal responses when excessive exercise interferes with the body’s usual adaptations to training. Such work could help clarify how beneficial physical activity progresses into a state of insufficient recovery and impaired performance.

articles.title: US wildfire damage is on pace to triple by mid-century, but there are affordable ways to lower the risk
articles.dek: As temperatures rise and development expands, the number of homes and other structures damaged or destroyed by wildfires across the U.
paragraphs: As temperatures rise and development expands, the number of homes and other structures damaged or destroyed by wildfires across the U. S. is on pace to triple by mid-century , my colleagues and I found in a study just published.

The 2026 wildfire season has been a sharp reminder of that risk and why making homes and properties less vulnerable to wildfires is increasingly crucial. Fortunately, strategies to lower the risk of losing a home to wildfire don’t have to be overly expensive .

The 2026 wildfire season began with historically low mountain snowpack , early snowmelt and exceptional warmth across much of the West. Even before the nation’s hottest summer on record intensified drought and dried vegetation, fires were breaking out.

Colorado’s Aspen Acres Fire destroyed hundreds of structures in June. Four firefighters died from injuries suffered when the fast-moving Knowles Fire overtook them near the Colorado–Utah border in July. In August, wind-driven fires swept into neighborhoods in Spokane, Washington , damaging more than 800 homes and forcing tens of thousands of residents to evacuate.

In Colorado, the summer monsoon season brought rainfall, helping firefighters gain ground. Across the Rocky Mountain region, lightning continued to start fires, but rain helped keep many fires small in many areas despite above-average temperatures.

Despite this reprieve, Colorado fires had burned more than 318,000 acres by late October, nearly twice the annual average since 2000. Nationally, the total area burned was also well above average . The U. S. spent 48 consecutive days at Preparedness Level 5 – the highest level, indicating that firefighting resources were stretched nationally – compared with a 10-year average of 25 days annually.

Fire is a natural and often beneficial part of many ecosystems, shaping vegetation and supporting biodiversity. However, a century of fire suppression has allowed dry vegetation to accumulate in forests that historically had frequently burned.

Rising temperatures caused by human activities such as burning fossil fuels have increased the rate at which the atmosphere pulls moisture from the land, drying soils and vegetation. Researchers estimate that this drying nearly doubled the area burned in western U. S. forests between 1984 and 2015 compared with what would have burned without human-caused climate change.

More people also now live in and at the edges of wildland areas , raising the risk of fires reaching neighborhoods. Human activity has extended the fire season beyond summer, when most lightning-caused fires occur, too. Power lines, vehicles, machinery, burning of debris and campfires can spark fires year-round.
These interacting factors have helped nearly quadruple the annual area burned in the western United States since 2000.
They also contribute to the growing threat of fast-growing fires , which can overwhelm emergency response.

In a 2024 study, my colleagues and I used satellite imagery to measure daily fire growth across the contiguous United States from 2001 to 2020. “Fast fires,” defined as those that burned more than 4,000 acres in a single day, represented just 2. 7% of fires analyzed but accounted for 78% of documented structures destroyed and 61% of reported firefighting costs.

A brief burst of growth, often fueled by strong winds or highly flammable materials, can matter enormously, even if a fire’s eventual size is relatively small. And in many ecosystems, fires are getting faster.
The number of people and buildings in harm’s way has also been increasing in the U. S. , raising the risk of damage.

Between 1945 and 2015, development in regions of the country with the highest wildfire risk expanded tenfold , increasing the amount of human exposure to wildfires while also introducing ignition sources and buildings that can burn. Once embers enter a neighborhood, fire can spread quickly from building to building.

My team’s new research suggests that without further action to reduce wildfire risk, the annual number of structures damaged or destroyed nationwide could nearly triple by mid-century. That would mean up to 449,000 structures lost between 2026 and 2060.

We used historical data about development patterns, wildfire area and the fires’ effects to reconstruct the past fire risk, then modeled future fire risk by incorporating weather, climate and housing-density expectations.

We found that roughly one-third of western neighborhoods facing the greatest future risk are low-income communities . In these communities, people may struggle to afford measures to protect their homes, maintain insurance coverage and recover financially after a fire.
These projections are sobering, but actual losses will depend partly on the choices people make now.

For example, homes can be made less likely to ignite with Class A fire-resistant roofs and ember-resistant vents that reduce the potential for burning particles to enter homes. Removing flammable debris , mulch, firewood and vegetation from around buildings also reduces the risk of fire spreading to the home. Community programs are available in many areas to help low-income homeowners reduce their home’s fire risk.

Building homes to be wildfire-resilient can also cost less than people may expect. In a study of new home construction, my colleagues and I found that meeting the two protection levels established by the Colorado fire code increased minimum construction costs by approximately 0. 6% and 4. 2%. Access to lower-cost materials and homeowner education can help make wildfire resilience more affordable.
Wildfire-resilient construction can lower the risk of losing a home, but it does not completely eliminate it.

Beyond individual buildings, prescribed burning and appropriately designed forest-thinning operations can reduce fuels and alter fire behavior before flames reach neighborhoods. Utilities can strengthen infrastructure and reduce the probability of ignition while limiting disruptions from preventive power shut-offs. Insurance companies can reward measurable risk reduction and help sustain coverage in communities working to become safer.

These measures work best when they reinforce one another . The odds of losing a home to wildfire depend on its construction, its immediate surroundings and the broader neighborhood. There is no one-size-fits-all solution to wildfire risk. As the threat grows, strategies tailored to the environmental, social and economic realities of each community are more important than ever.

articles.title: The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season
articles.dek: Tropical cyclone activity in the Northwest Pacific Basin has been elevated since April 2026, when Sinlaku surged to super typhoon strength and battered Micronesia, Guam, and…
paragraphs: Tropical cyclone activity in the Northwest Pacific Basin has been elevated since April 2026, when Sinlaku surged to super typhoon strength and battered Micronesia, Guam, and the Northern Mariana Islands. Twenty-five named storms later, the basin still hummed with activity in late October.

When the EPIC (Earth Polychromatic Imaging Camera) on the DSCOVR (Deep Space Climate Observatory) satellite captured this image (above) on October 29, 2026, Super Typhoon In-fa churned near the Mariana Islands. At the same time, the remnants of Typhoon Champi approached Alaska amid a parade of storms moving across the Bering Sea. In-fa is the fifth typhoon to affect the Mariana Islands this year.

The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite captured the image of In-fa below on October 30, when the storm was just west of the island chain. In-fa was unusually intense at the time of the image, with a nearly circular shape and large eye—a collection of characteristics that meteorologists use to identify a subset of tropical cyclones known as annular storms . These storms typically lack prominent outer spiral-shaped rainbands—a common feature of standard tropical cyclones—which is why meteorologists have a habit of calling annular storms “doughnuts” or “truck tires.”

Annular storms are rare, accounting for just 4 percent of tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific, according to one analysis . Their eyes average about 45 kilometers (30 miles) in diameter, compared to about 25 kilometers for standard tropical cyclones, and the storms typically maintain their strength longer in unfavorable conditions.

In-fa was still a tropical cyclone when EPIC captured the image at the top of the page, but Champi’s leftovers had gone through the process of extratropical transition and become a whole different type of storm as they entered the Bering Sea’s busy storm track. Tropical cyclones are warm-core storms fueled by the heat and moisture of warm ocean water, but extratropical cyclones typically have cold cores and draw energy from temperature contrasts between warm and cold air masses.

Unlike tropical cyclones, extratropical cyclones typically develop fronts and huge, spiraling cloud bands shaped like commas . “One of the calling cards of extratropical transitions is the expansion of a storm’s wind field,” said Gary Partyka, a meteorologist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. “It’s not that the winds necessarily grow stronger, but they cover a much larger area,” he said.

In this case, there likely would still have been a midlatitude storm over the Bering Sea, possibly with large, comma-shaped clouds on October 30, even without Champi’s remnants, he added. “But it looks like Champi became intertwined with and helped intensify that system,” he said.

Champi’s transformation came after a long and destructive tour through the West Pacific, during which the typhoon achieved maximum sustained winds of nearly 300 kilometers (185 miles) per hour, prompting some observers to call it one of the strongest storms of the season.

Despite narrowly skirting Taiwan and Guam, the powerhouse storm brought damaging winds and intense rains to both places, as well as to parts of China and Japan. When the remnants hit Alaska, the state avoided catastrophic damage on the scale of what happened after ex-typhoon Halong struck in October 2025 , but some areas did see high winds and heavy rain and snowfall, according to news reports .

Champi is the fourth ex-typhoon to enter Alaskan waters this year, noted University of Alaska Fairbanks meteorologist and climatologist Rick Thoman , following Bang-Lang in August, Dujuan in September, and Choi-wan in early October. The autumns of 1997 and 2015—both very strong El Niño years—had three each, he added. Roughly 60 ex-typhoons have impacted the state since 1970 , according to Thoman.

Partyka described 2026 as a “particularly active year” for Pacific tropical cyclones, increasing the chances that Alaska would be affected by storms that have gone through extratropical transitions. The strong El Niño underway in the Pacific is a “likely contributor” to the increased activity, he added.

articles.title: Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now
articles.dek: Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight.
paragraphs: Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis.

Today, Johnson serves as NASA’s Center of Excellence for Human Spaceflight, and its workforce is helping to usher in a Golden Age of innovation and discovery. Johnson is home to America’s astronaut corps, the Mission Control Center, and the teams behind some of humanity’s greatest achievements in space. As NASA’s human spaceflight programs evolve, Johnson remains at the forefront of these efforts.

Houston is home to NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, comprising International Space Station operations and commercial partnerships and destinations in low Earth orbit. For missions beyond low Earth orbit, Johnson houses the Moon Base Program⁠ and Orion Program⁠ , while NASA’s Human Health and Performance Directorate⁠ and Human Research Program ⁠ work to protect crew health and performance as missions extend farther from Earth.

On May 25, 1961, the center’s story began when President John F. Kennedy gave a speech before a joint session of Congress, committing the nation to achieve the goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the end of the decade.

NASA’s Space Task Group, in charge of America’s human spaceflight program, was already working on Project Mercury to put astronauts into Earth orbit, but with the additional task of a human lunar landing, it soon outgrew its facilities at NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The agency decided it needed a dedicated field center for human spaceflight and on Sept. 19, 1961, after evaluating multiple sites around the country, NASA announced that the new Manned Spacecraft Center would be built near Houston, Texas. The agency established the center on Nov. 1, 1961, and construction began in 1962. In 1973, it officially became NASA’s Lyndon B.
Johnson Space Center in honor of President Johnson for his ardent support of America’s space program from its foundation.

The Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, and while construction continued on the Clear Lake site, employees worked in 13 leased buildings in southeast Houston. The design phase took six months and construction of the first buildings took 18 months, with the first employees moving onto the new site in late 1963.
Over the decades, the number of buildings grew, and continues to grow, to meet the demands of new spaceflight programs.

Construction of the nine-story Project Management Building began on Dec. 5, 1962, and concluded on March 15, 1964. Robert Gilruth , the center’s first director, moved into his office on March 5, 1964, on the top floor of the edifice then known as Building 2. The building swapped numbers with the Public Affairs Building, originally known as Building 1, on June 30, 1974.

The use of neutral buoyancy for spacewalk training began with the Gemini XII mission in 1966. In 1967, workers installed an above-ground circular pool called the Water Immersion Facility for astronaut training that supported Apollo and pre-Shuttle spacewalk training.. To accommodate the larger size of the space shuttle payload bay, spacewalk training moved to the Weightless Environment Training Facility iin 1980. Astronauts used it for nearly all shuttle spacewalk training until 1997, when the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in the Sonny Carter Training Center entered operations for both shuttle and space station training, as well as testing future space suits and lunar surface activities.

To prevent any back contamination from any possible lunar microorganisms, NASA designed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Building 37. Construction began in August 1966, with the first employees moving into their offices in June 1967. The astronauts from Apollo 11, 12, and 14 completed their three-week postflight quarantine in the lab, and scientists in the various laboratories studied the lunar samples all the Apollo missions returned.

Following the Apollo program, Life Sciences division and laboratories moved into the building until they relocated in 2017. Following demolition of Building 37, the Lunar Receiving Park, dedicated in 2026, honors the history of the laboratory.

For missions beyond low Earth orbit, Johnson houses the Moon Base Program⁠ and Orion Program⁠ , while NASA’s Human Health and Performance Directorate⁠ and Human Research Program ⁠ work to protect crew health and performance as missions extend farther from Earth.

On May 25, 1961, the center’s story began when President John F. Kennedy gave a speech before a joint session of Congress, committing the nation to achieve the goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the end of the decade.

NASA’s Space Task Group, in charge of America’s human spaceflight program, was already working on Project Mercury to put astronauts into Earth orbit, but with the additional task of a human lunar landing, it soon outgrew its facilities at NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The agency decided it needed a dedicated field center for human spaceflight and on Sept. 19, 1961, after evaluating multiple sites around the country, NASA announced that the new Manned Spacecraft Center would be built near Houston, Texas. The agency established the center on Nov. 1, 1961, and construction began in 1962. In 1973, it officially became NASA’s Lyndon B.
Johnson Space Center in honor of President Johnson for his ardent support of America’s space program from its foundation.

The Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, and while construction continued on the Clear Lake site, employees worked in 13 leased buildings in southeast Houston. The design phase took six months and construction of the first buildings took 18 months, with the first employees moving onto the new site in late 1963.
Over the decades, the number of buildings grew, and continues to grow, to meet the demands of new spaceflight programs.

Construction of the nine-story Project Management Building began on Dec. 5, 1962, and concluded on March 15, 1964. Robert Gilruth , the center’s first director, moved into his office on March 5, 1964, on the top floor of the edifice then known as Building 2. The building swapped numbers with the Public Affairs Building, originally known as Building 1, on June 30, 1974.

The use of neutral buoyancy for spacewalk training began with the Gemini XII mission in 1966. In 1967, workers installed an above-ground circular pool called the Water Immersion Facility for astronaut training that supported Apollo and pre-Shuttle spacewalk training.. To accommodate the larger size of the space shuttle payload bay, spacewalk training moved to the Weightless Environment Training Facility iin 1980. Astronauts used it for nearly all shuttle spacewalk training until 1997, when the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in the Sonny Carter Training Center entered operations for both shuttle and space station training, as well as testing future space suits and lunar surface activities.

To prevent any back contamination from any possible lunar microorganisms, NASA designed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Building 37. Construction began in August 1966, with the first employees moving into their offices in June 1967. The astronauts from Apollo 11, 12, and 14 completed their three-week postflight quarantine in the lab, and scientists in the various laboratories studied the lunar samples all the Apollo missions returned.

Following the Apollo program, Life Sciences division and laboratories moved into the building until they relocated in 2017. Following demolition of Building 37, the Lunar Receiving Park, dedicated in 2026, honors the history of the laboratory.

articles.title: What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA
articles.dek: Catch Taurid and Leonid meteors, spot Mars near Jupiter, celebrate Voyager 1’s light-day milestone, and watch November’s supermoon.
paragraphs: Catch Taurid and Leonid meteors, spot Mars near Jupiter, celebrate Voyager 1’s light-day milestone, and watch November’s supermoon.
A month of meteor showers … a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter … and a supermoon!
November offers a buffet of opportunities to see a meteor streak across the sky!
The Southern Taurids peak around November 5th, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12th.
Those names refer to the two areas in the constellation Taurus, where the meteors appear to originate.
Each Taurid shower produces only a handful of meteors per hour—around five, under ideal conditions—but an occasional bright fireball can make the wait worthwhile.

Next up are the Leonids. For the best viewing times, try the early morning hours of November 17th and 18th, after the Moon sets. Under ideal conditions, the shower could produce around 15 meteors per hour, though most viewers will see fewer.
To level up your viewing experience, you will want to find a dark location, give your eyes about half an hour to adjust, and take in as much sky as you can.
Around mid-month, there’s another reason to head outside early. On the mornings of November 15th and 16th, look southeast before sunrise to see Mars and Jupiter close together.
They’ll appear about 1. 2 degrees apart—a little more than the width of two full Moons side by side. Jupiter is the brighter point of light, with reddish Mars nearby.
Both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye. They’re still far apart in space, but from Earth, they appear almost side by side.
Watch over several mornings to see them draw closer together – and then go their separate ways.
This month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft will reach a historic milestone, becoming the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth.
That means a signal traveling at the speed of light takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft – and another 24 hours for us to hear back from it!

articles.title: NASA Invites Media to Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Station Resupply Launch
articles.dek: Media accreditation is open for the next launch to deliver NASA science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station.
paragraphs: Media accreditation is open for the next launch to deliver NASA science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. A Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft will launch in November to the orbital laboratory on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket for NASA.

The mission is known as NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25, or NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25. Liftoff is targeted for no earlier than 10:49 a. m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

Following launch, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 robotic arm to capture Cygnus and install the spacecraft to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading. The spacecraft will remain at the space station until May 2027. This is the company’s 25th spacecraft built to deliver supplies to the International Space Station under contract with NASA.

Credentialing to cover prelaunch and launch activities is open to U. S. media. The application deadline for U. S. citizens is 11:59 p. m. EST, Thursday, Nov. 12. All accreditation requests must be submitted online at:

Credentialed media will receive a confirmation email following approval. NASA’s media accreditation policy is available online. For questions about accreditation, or to request special logistical support, email: ksc-media-accreditat@mail. nasa. gov. For other questions, please contact NASA’s Kennedy Space Center newsroom at: 321-867-2468.

In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several new experiments, including hardware to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles in space that could improve drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis, as well as a study that could guide cancer treatments by predicting whether a patient’s cancer is likely to spread to other parts of the body. Cygnus also will carry human muscle cells and medications to test therapeutics for muscle loss associated with spaceflight and aging on Earth, and a compact radiation sensor designed to improve crew safety on future missions.

Each resupply mission to the station delivers scientific investigations in the areas of biology and biotechnology, Earth and space science, physical sciences, and technology development and demonstrations. Cargo resupply from U. S. companies ensures a national capability to deliver scientific research to the space station, increasing NASA’s ability to conduct new investigations aboard humanity’s laboratory in space.

For 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs that are not possible on Earth. The space station is an important testbed for NASA to understand and overcome the challenges of long-duration spaceflight and to expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit. As commercial companies concentrate on providing human space transportation services and destinations as part of a strong low Earth orbit economy , NASA is focusing its resources on deep space missions to the Moon as part of the Artemis and Moon Base programs to build on our foundation for the first astronaut missions to Mars.

articles.title: Not in a FEMA flood zone? Your home could still be at risk – and you could suffer more than your neighbor
articles.dek: If your home isn’t in a federally designated flood zone, flooding might seem like someone else’s problem.
paragraphs: If your home isn’t in a federally designated flood zone, flooding might seem like someone else’s problem. No one requires you to buy flood insurance, and the map suggests you’re in the clear. But reality may be very different.

Mounting evidence reveals that significantly more homes are at risk of flooding than is indicated by FEMA’s 100-year flood maps – about 6 million more , and 14. 6 million properties in all, by one estimate. The official maps are commonly outdated , and some are two decades old . Even when updated, they typically rely on historical flood data rather than future risk projections.
But there’s another problem that redrawing the lines won’t solve.
FEMA’s flood maps answer only one question: Is the water likely to reach my neighborhood? They don’t assess an individual home’s risks or what the impacts are likely to be when the water rises.
To understand the impact, more comprehensive data is needed , including the probable flood depth at the home, the building’s age and construction quality, and insurance coverage.
When these other factors are considered, your home’s true flood risk is far more complex than the map might seem to indicate.
The data shows how two houses on the same street can face radically different risks from flooding , even when located in the same flood zone – and where local governments can help.

One home may be newer, well maintained and covered by flood insurance. Another may be decades older, at the low end of the same street where water runs deeper during a flood, and is in poor repair and uninsured. The same storm would leave them in very different predicaments, with very different paths to recovery.

Neighborhood averages can make it hard to tell which homes are likely to be hit hardest. But understanding an individual property’s risks matters for residents figuring out how to protect a home, and for local officials deciding where limited flood-protection money should go.

We study how flooding affects homes and the people who live in them. To see how much these house-by-house differences matter, we and colleagues Aaron Flores of Arizona State University and Sara Meerow of the University of Colorado Boulder built a detailed flood risk score for nearly 1 million homes in Houston. We describe the results in a new study published in the journal Applied Geography.

Our past research in Houston found that more than half of 100,000 documented flood-prone buildings in the city currently lie outside official flood boundaries, and that these overlooked buildings are more likely to be in poor condition and uninsured, leaving them especially exposed when the floodwaters do come.
To get a better understanding of each household’s vulnerability, we combined four types of information about each home.

We chose these four criteria because flood research consistently highlights their importance for how hard a flood hits a community: how much water arrives , how well the building holds up , whether people can still get around and how big the repair bill is for the owner . They aren’t the only possible measures; a city could use others within each category, depending on available data.

Homes in the same neighborhood can have very different flood vulnerability scores. In fact, we found the scores differed more from house to house within a neighborhood than from one neighborhood to the next.

In practice, this means that knowing a neighborhood’s flood risk doesn’t necessarily tell you how hard a flood could hit any individual home. A neighborhood could look safe on average while containing some of the county’s riskiest homes , and there may be many well-protected homes in an otherwise risky neighborhood. Much of the problem, we show, lies at the scale of buildings, not neighborhoods or ZIP codes.
Homeowners can check several of these risks themselves.

Ask longtime neighbors or your city’s flood plain office whether your home or the street has been flooded before. Look up the home’s age in local property records and have an inspector assess its condition. Find out whether the routes to work and school flood easily. And check whether you have a flood insurance policy , and what it covers: Most homeowner’s policies don’t cover flood damage.

Communities can apply our approach with their own data to locate particularly vulnerable housing where neighborhood averages may disguise the need for help. They can start with existing address-level flood scores, such as First Street’s , and add local records on buildings, roads and insurance. The extra details matter because officials have limited money for flood-proofing homes , improving drainage and helping families recover after floods. Better data on buildings and flood risk can help them invest wisely.
Data similar to that used for Houston exists across much of the United States, so other flood-prone cities could follow the same approach.
Floods don’t stop at the lines on a map, and they don’t hit every house on a street the same. We believe it’s time for residents and local flood authorities to prepare accordingly.
